title: Which of these first three claims about values are right?
description: Three claims about the values of expressions are checked by putting the given number in place of the letter. Keeko doubts the first check and drops the minus sign of the number.
teaching_notes: One idea: to check a claim, put the number in place of the letter, keep its sign, multiply first, and compare the true value with the claim. Watch for students who drop the minus sign of a negative number.

source: Check these claims. 1: if a = −4, then 10 − a = 6. 2: if d = 6, then 3d = 36. 3: if s = 7, then 3s − 2 = 15.
video_script.why: A learner sees that a claim about the value of an expression is checked by putting in the number, keeping its sign, and working out the true value.
video_script.substitution: The book's own three claims, checked one by one.
video_script.anchor: three claims, each with an expression, a number for its letter, and a stated value
video_script.wrong_answer: ten minus eigh with eigh as minus four is six
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko drops the minus sign of the number, so 10 − 4 = 6, but 10 − (−4) = 10 + 4 = 14.

final_answer.spoken: the true values are fourteen, eighteen and nineteen, so all three claims are wrong

never_show: the three true values together before the answer beat
video_script.design: One idea: put the number in place of the letter, keep its sign, and compare. Assumes the value of an expression for a given number. The three claims stay on the stage and each is crossed out when it fails. Wrong idea: drop the minus sign of the number.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; three cards, each holding a claim about the value of an expression for a given number

marks.p1: the title card From your book arrives
marks.p2: three cards appear, each with a claim
marks.p3: the letter, its number and the stated value are highlighted on each card
marks.p4: a question mark glows over the three cards

narration: <bookmark mark='p1'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='p2'/>It gives three claims about the values of expressions.
<bookmark mark='p3'/>Each claim names a letter, the number it stands for, and a value.
<bookmark mark='p4'/>Which of the claims are right?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a claim card; a number tile with its sign slides into the slot of a letter; the true value is compared with the stated value

marks.g1: a number tile slides into the slot where the letter sits
marks.g2: the sign of the number stays glued to its tile
marks.g3: the true value and the stated value are placed side by side

narration: <bookmark mark='g1'/>To check a claim, we put the number in place of the letter.
<bookmark mark='g2'/>Then we work out the value, and keep the sign of the number.
<bookmark mark='g3'/>If our value is not the stated value, the claim is wrong.

beats.on_screen: Given: 1: if a = −4, then 10 − a = 6 ; 2: if d = 6, then 3d = 36 ; 3: if s = 7, then 3s − 2 = 15

marks.gv2: the second claim is written under it
marks.gv3: the third claim is written under that

narration: <bookmark mark='gv1'/>Given, the first claim says ten minus eigh is six, when eigh is minus four.
<bookmark mark='gv2'/>The second says three d is thirty six, when d is six.
<bookmark mark='gv3'/>The third says three s minus two is fifteen, when s is seven.

beats.on_screen: To find: the true value in each claim, and whether the claim is right
narration: <bookmark mark='fd1'/>We find the true value in each claim, and see if the claim is right.

marks.s1a: −4 is put in place of a, inside a bracket

narration: <bookmark mark='s1a'/>For the first claim, put minus four in place of eigh.
<bookmark mark='s1b'/>Ten minus the number minus four becomes ten plus four.
<bookmark mark='s1c'/>That is fourteen, so the first claim is not right.

marks.s2a: 3d opens up to 3 × d and 6 is put in place of d

narration: <bookmark mark='s2a'/>In the second claim, three d means three times d.
<bookmark mark='s2b'/>Three times six is eighteen, so the second claim is not right either.
<bookmark mark='s3a'/>In the third claim, multiplication comes first, so three times seven is twenty one.
<bookmark mark='s3b'/>Twenty one minus two is nineteen, so the third claim is not right either.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 1: 14, 2: 18, 3: 19. All three claims are wrong

marks.ans: all three claims are crossed out
marks.ans2: the three true values are boxed together

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>All three claims are wrong.
<bookmark mark='ans2'/>The true values are fourteen, eighteen and nineteen.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

marks.d2: the minus sign of the number is shown glued to its tile
marks.d3: the bubble is struck out and 10 − (−4) = 10 + 4 is written beside it

narration: <bookmark mark='d1'/>Keeko thinks ten minus eigh with eigh as minus four is six. The minus sign of the four is dropped.
<bookmark mark='d2'/>But the sign belongs to the number, so it must stay when we put the number in.
<bookmark mark='d3'/>Taking away minus four adds four, so the value is fourteen, not six.
